topic: Waves in air, fluids and solids: Waves for detection and exploration (physics only) (HT only)
subject: physics

items.q: A survey team sends waves down into the ground to look for a buried rock layer in which the waves would travel at a different speed. What happens when the waves reach the top of that buried layer?
items.correct: Part of each wave is reflected back and the rest travels on
items.misconception: The waves carry on downwards at exactly the same speed
items.why: Students meet a single quoted value for the speed of sound, or for the speed of light, early on and store it as a property of the wave rather than of the wave in one particular medium. Speeds in solids and liquids are rarely quoted beside it. Velocity is the first of the three differences this statement names. It is precisely because the wave travels at a different speed in the hidden material that a boundary reflects part of the wave at all, and the right speed for that medium must be used whenever a time is turned into a distance.
items.random_wrong: All of each wave is reflected and none of it travels on

items.q: Survey waves pass easily through rock layer X but are strongly absorbed by rock layer Y. How does this difference help the team explore ground they cannot see?
items.correct: A weak returning signal shows the waves went through layer Y
items.misconception: Strong absorption sends back a stronger reflection from layer Y
items.why: Both words describe something happening to a wave at or inside a material, and students who have not separated the two energy pathways treat them as interchangeable descriptions of the wave being 'stopped'. The specification lists absorption and reflection as separate differences. Reflection sends part of the wave back; absorption removes energy from the wave altogether. A strongly absorbing layer returns a weak signal, and that weakness is itself the clue to what the layer is.
items.random_wrong: Layer Y reflects every wave, so nothing returns from below

items.q: Which statement about ultrasound waves is correct?
items.correct: Their frequency is above the highest frequency a person hears
items.misconception: Their frequency is below the lowest frequency a person hears
items.why: Students remember that ultrasound lies outside the audible range but not which end of it. Documentary facts about elephants and whales using very low sounds supply a vivid wrong anchor. The specification is explicit: ultrasound waves have a frequency higher than the upper limit of hearing for humans. Sound below the lower limit is infrasound, which this specification does not require.
items.random_wrong: They are electromagnetic waves, like the X-rays used in hospitals

items.q: An ultrasound pulse travelling through soft tissue meets a boundary with bone. What happens to the pulse at that boundary?
items.correct: Part of it is reflected, part carries on
items.misconception: All of it bounces back and none enters the bone
items.why: Reflection is first taught with mirrors, where effectively all the light comes back, and transmission with clear glass, where effectively all of it goes through. Students carry over the two extreme cases and have no picture of a boundary doing both at once. The specification says ultrasound waves are partially reflected at a boundary. Partial reflection is what makes imaging possible: the reflected part reveals that boundary, and the transmitted part travels on to reveal the next one.
items.random_wrong: None of it comes back; it all enters the bone

items.q: An ultrasound pulse leaves a probe on a patient's skin and travels at 1500 m/s. The reflection from a boundary inside the body is detected 0.001 s after the pulse leaves the probe. How far is that boundary from the probe?
items.why: Students apply distance travelled = speed × time correctly and then stop, because nothing in the arithmetic itself reminds them that the pulse made a return journey. The specification says the time taken is for the reflections to reach a detector. Speed × time gives the whole there-and-back path; halve it to get the distance to the boundary.

items.q: A ship measures water depth by echo sounding. It records the time between sending a sound pulse downwards and detecting the echo. How is the depth found from that time?
items.correct: Multiply the time by the speed of sound, then halve it
items.misconception: Multiply the time by the speed of sound in water
items.why: Students apply distance travelled = speed × time correctly and then stop, because nothing in the arithmetic itself reminds them that the pulse made a return journey. The specification says the time taken is for the reflections to reach a detector. Speed × time gives the whole there-and-back path; halve it to get the distance to the boundary.
items.random_wrong: Divide the speed of sound in water by that time

items.q: Echo sounding uses high frequency sound waves rather than light or radio waves. Why is sound the wave that is used?
items.correct: Water absorbs light and radio waves in a short distance
items.misconception: Sound travels faster through deep sea water than light does
items.why: Students know sound travels faster in water than in air and mistakenly extend the comparison to light, helped by the fact that light obviously does not get far down into deep water. The reason is absorption, not speed. Light and radio waves are absorbed by water over short distances; high frequency sound is not, so it reaches the sea bed and returns.
items.random_wrong: Any wave would work here; sound is just the usual choice

items.q: Which statement about P-waves and S-waves is correct?
items.correct: P-waves are longitudinal, S-waves transverse
items.misconception: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal
items.why: The two letters carry no obvious meaning for students, so the pairing is memorised without a hook and is as easily recalled backwards as forwards. Transverse is also the picture students draw for almost every wave. P-waves are longitudinal, S-waves are transverse. The distinction matters because it is the transverse S-wave that cannot travel through a liquid, which is the whole basis of the evidence about the core.
items.random_wrong: Both P-waves and S-waves are longitudinal waves

items.q: After an earthquake, detectors on the far side of the Earth record P-waves but no S-waves. What does this indicate about the Earth's core?
items.correct: Part of the core is liquid: S-waves cannot pass through liquid
items.misconception: No seismic wave of any kind can pass through the core
items.why: The memorable fact is that something is blocked, and the qualifier 'S-waves only' is the part that drops away. Picturing a liquid as an obstacle also feels intuitive. The specification says S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, and separately that P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids — which means P-waves do travel through them. That contrast is exactly what makes the evidence work.
items.random_wrong: There is an empty gap inside the Earth stopping the S-waves

items.q: P-waves travel at different speeds through solids and liquids. How does this provide evidence about the Earth's core?
items.correct: Where their speed changes shows where the core begins and ends
items.misconception: P-waves keep one fixed speed, so arrival times give distance only
items.why: Students meet a single quoted value for the speed of sound, or for the speed of light, early on and store it as a property of the wave rather than of the wave in one particular medium. Speeds in solids and liquids are rarely quoted beside it. Velocity is the first of the three differences this statement names. It is precisely because the wave travels at a different speed in the hidden material that a boundary reflects part of the wave at all, and the right speed for that medium must be used whenever a time is turned into a distance.
items.random_wrong: P-waves are absorbed by the core, so a shadow shows its size

items.q: A P-wave travels through solid rock. How does the rock itself move as the wave passes through it?
items.correct: The rock vibrates back and forth in the direction of travel
items.misconception: The rock is carried bodily along with the wave as it travels
items.why: Earthquake footage shows ground visibly moving and objects being displaced, which looks like material being carried along. The idea that a wave transfers energy without transferring matter is abstract by comparison. A P-wave is longitudinal: each part of the rock oscillates back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels, then returns. The energy moves on through the Earth; the rock stays where it is.
items.random_wrong: The rock moves from side to side across the direction of travel

items.q: The study of seismic waves led to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable. What did the seismic waves provide?
items.correct: Evidence about material that nobody has seen
items.misconception: Confirmation of what deep drilling had already shown
items.why: Students know that rock samples and boreholes exist and do not appreciate the difference in scale between the deepest borehole and the depth of the core. The specification's point is that these parts of the Earth are not directly observable. Seismic waves provided new evidence about a region no one has ever sampled or seen.
items.random_wrong: Ideas about the deep Earth that can never be tested

items.q: Is ultrasound a type of electromagnetic radiation?
items.correct: No. Ultrasound is sound: a longitudinal wave that needs a medium to travel through.
items.misconception: Ultrasound must be a form of radiation like X-rays, because it is used in hospitals to see inside people.
items.why: Every other hospital imaging method students have heard of uses electromagnetic radiation, so the hospital setting, not the physics, drives the classification. The prefix 'ultra' also echoes 'ultraviolet'. Ultrasound is defined by its frequency being above the upper limit of human hearing, which only makes sense for sound. It is a mechanical wave, cannot travel through a vacuum, and is not ionising.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is ultrasound simply sound that is too quiet, or too loud, for the ear to detect?
items.correct: No. What puts ultrasound outside the audible range is its frequency, not how loud or quiet it is.
items.misconception: Ultrasound is sound at a volume the human ear cannot cope with, so you cannot hear it however hard you listen.
items.why: Everyday talk about sound is almost entirely about loudness, and students who have not firmly separated amplitude from frequency reach for the property they use daily. The limits of hearing are limits of frequency. A loud ultrasound wave and a quiet one are both inaudible because the ear cannot respond to that frequency at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Should the halving for a there-and-back journey be applied twice?
items.correct: No. Halve once, and only once — either halve the time before multiplying, or halve the distance afterwards, but never both.
items.misconception: Because the pulse goes out and comes back, you halve the time and then halve the answer as well.
items.why: Students who have been drilled to 'remember to halve' apply the correction as a ritual rather than tracking the journey, so it gets used at both of the available opportunities. There is one return journey, so there is one factor of two. Halving the time gives the one-way travel time, which already yields the one-way distance; halving that again gives an answer four times too small.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are P-waves and S-waves two names for the same kind of wave?
items.correct: No. They are different types of wave — one longitudinal, one transverse — which is why they behave differently deep inside the Earth.
items.misconception: P-waves and S-waves are both the same type of seismic wave, differing only in when they arrive.
items.why: Both are produced by the same earthquake and recorded on the same trace, so the obvious difference — that one arrives before the other — is taken to be the only difference. The specification names the type of each separately. If they were the same type they would be stopped by the same things, and there would be no S-wave evidence about the core at all.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If no S-waves arrive from beyond the core, is there an empty space inside the Earth?
items.correct: No. The S-waves are stopped because the material there is liquid, not because there is nothing there.
items.misconception: Missing S-waves show there is a hollow gap or empty space deep inside the Earth.
items.why: Students reason that if the waves have stopped there must be nothing to carry them, and 'nothing' is read as empty space rather than as the wrong sort of something. A liquid is a medium; it carries the longitudinal P-wave perfectly well. What it cannot carry is a transverse wave. Missing S-waves are therefore evidence of liquid, and the region in which they are missing indicates the size of that liquid part.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do S-waves fail to arrive on the far side simply because they have faded away?
items.correct: No. If distance alone were the reason, the P-waves that travelled just as far would be missing too.
items.misconception: S-waves are weaker, so they die out before they can reach detectors on the far side of the Earth.
items.why: Absorption over distance is a genuine effect students have met, so it is a ready-made explanation for any wave that fails to arrive, and it needs no thought about the material on the path. P-waves from the same earthquake do arrive on the far side, so the path length is not the problem. The specification gives the reason directly: S-waves cannot travel through a liquid.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Could light or radio waves be used instead of sound for echo sounding?
items.correct: No, not usefully. Light and radio waves are absorbed within a short distance in water, so they cannot reach the sea bed and return.
items.misconception: Any wave would do the job equally well; sound is used only because it is traditional.
items.why: Radar and echo sounding are described in the same words — send a pulse, time the echo — so students see the two as interchangeable and never ask what the water does to each wave. This is exactly the use of absorption the specification asks about. Sound travels a long way through water while light and radio waves do not, so sound is the wave that can carry information back from deep water.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If part of the Earth cannot be observed directly, can anything really be known about it?
items.correct: Yes. Indirect evidence — measuring what waves do after passing through a region — supports firm and testable conclusions about it.
items.misconception: Anything you cannot see for yourself is guesswork, so claims about the deep Earth can never be tested.
items.why: Students equate evidence with seeing. Indirect measurement is unfamiliar as a form of proof, so a conclusion drawn from it feels like an opinion. The specification records that seismic waves provided new evidence leading to discoveries about parts of the Earth which are not directly observable. Predictions made from that evidence are tested against every new earthquake recorded.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
